## 1. Purpose

This procedure describes the determination of soil bulk density using
the volumetric core method. Bulk density ($\rho_b$) is the mass of
oven-dried soil per unit volume of field-moist soil, expressed in
g/cm^3^. It is used to convert gravimetric measurements (e.g., nutrient
concentrations in mg/kg) to volumetric or areal bases (e.g., kg/ha),
to assess soil compaction, to calculate total porosity, and to evaluate
management effects on soil physical quality. The core method is the
most widely used direct measurement of bulk density and is described
in the SSSA Methods of Soil Analysis [@blake1986; @grossman2002].


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Mineral soils at all EA Program field sites, including
  agricultural plots, photovoltaic panel study sites, and restoration
  sites. Suitable for depths of 0--30 cm using hand-driven cores.
- **Does not apply to:** Soils with abundant coarse fragments (greater
  than approximately 20% by volume of gravel, cobbles, or stones),
  which require the excavation or clod method. Also not applicable to
  organic soils (histosols) or very loose sandy soils where core
  insertion causes compaction of the sample.
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites; laboratory drying and
  weighing in SGM 133


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                              |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| Lab PI            | Approve sampling plan, ensure training compliance |
| Field Lead        | Coordinate sampling logistics, verify equipment |
| Trained Personnel | Collect cores and process samples per this SOP |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent sampling |


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Physical:** Driving the core sampler with a mallet or hammer poses
  a risk of hand and finger injury. Trowels and soil knives are sharp.
  Repetitive hammering can cause strain.
- **Biological:** Soil-borne pathogens; wash hands thoroughly after
  handling soil. Tick and insect exposure at field sites.
- **Environmental:** Standard field hazards (heat, uneven terrain, sun
  exposure).
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Nitrile or leather work gloves
- [ ] Safety glasses (when driving the sampler)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)

### Related SOPs

Refer to [SOP-F01 Field Safety](SOP-F01-field-safety.qmd) for general
field safety procedures, including transportation, weather hazards, and
emergency response.


## 5. Equipment and Materials

### Field Equipment

| Item                          | Notes                                     |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Bulk density core rings       | Known internal volume; typical dimensions: 5 cm height x 5 cm diameter (approximately 98 cm^3^) or 7.5 cm x 7.5 cm |
| Core sampler (drive head)     | Fits over the core ring; beveled cutting edge |
| Rubber mallet or dead-blow hammer | For driving the sampler                |
| Driving cap or block          | Wooden or rubber block to protect the sampler from mallet strikes |
| Flat-blade trowel or soil knife | For excavating around the core and trimming ends |
| Straight-edged blade or spatula | For trimming flush with ring ends        |
| Plastic caps or aluminum foil | Two per core, to seal both ends after trimming |
| Pre-labeled ziplock bags      | For transporting sealed cores             |
| Cooler with ice packs         | If gravimetric moisture will be determined separately |
| Ruler or depth gauge          | For measuring insertion depth              |
| Field notebook                | For recording site, depth, and core ID    |
| GPS unit or smartphone        | For recording sampling coordinates         |

### Laboratory Equipment

| Item                          | Notes                                     |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Drying oven                   | Set to 105 C; see [SOP-L16](../lab_sops/SOP-L16-drying-ovens.qmd) |
| Analytical balance            | 0.01 g resolution minimum; see [SOP-L13](../lab_sops/SOP-L13-using-balances.qmd) |
| Desiccator                    | For cooling dried samples before weighing |
| Pre-weighed aluminum drying tins | Large enough to hold the full core volume |
| Calipers or ruler             | For verifying core ring dimensions        |


## 6. Procedure

### 6.1 Pre-Sampling Preparation

1. Measure and record the internal dimensions of each core ring
   (inside diameter and height) using calipers. Calculate the volume:

$$
V = \pi \left(\frac{d}{2}\right)^2 \times h
$$

where $d$ = inside diameter (cm) and $h$ = height (cm).

2. Pre-label core rings or bags with site name, plot ID, depth, and
   replicate number
3. Pre-weigh aluminum drying tins and record the tare mass
4. Clean core rings and the sampler with DI water before use
5. File a field work planning form per
   [SOP-F01](SOP-F01-field-safety.qmd)

### 6.2 Field Sampling

1. Navigate to the predetermined sampling location and record GPS
   coordinates
2. Clear surface litter, loose organic debris, and any vegetation from
   a small area (approximately 15 x 15 cm) at the sampling point
   without disturbing the mineral soil surface

::: {.callout-important}
Do not compress or disturb the soil surface before inserting the core.
The goal is to capture the soil at its natural field density.
:::

3. Assemble the core ring inside the drive head. Ensure the beveled
   cutting edge faces downward.
4. Place the assembled sampler vertically on the soil surface
5. Position the driving cap or wooden block on top of the sampler
6. Drive the sampler into the soil using the mallet, applying steady,
   even blows. Drive until the top of the core ring is flush with, or
   slightly below, the soil surface.
7. Do not over-drive the sampler. If the ring is driven more than 1 cm
   past flush, the sample may be compacted and should be discarded.
8. Carefully excavate the soil around the sampler using the trowel,
   leaving a pedestal of soil beneath and around the core
9. Slide the trowel or soil knife beneath the bottom of the core to
   sever it from the underlying soil
10. Lift the sampler and core out of the ground

### 6.3 Trimming and Capping

1. Remove the core ring from the drive head
2. Using a straight-edged blade, trim the soil flush with the top and
   bottom of the ring. Remove any material that extends beyond the
   ring face. Be careful not to smear or compress the soil.
3. If large roots or rocks protrude from the core face, note this in
   the field notebook. If coarse fragments constitute a substantial
   fraction of the core, record this and consider whether the core
   method is appropriate for this site.
4. Cap both ends of the ring with plastic caps or wrap tightly with
   aluminum foil
5. Place the capped core in a labeled ziplock bag
6. Store in the cooler for transport to the laboratory

::: {.callout-tip}
### Tip
Collect a minimum of three replicate cores per plot or treatment to
account for spatial variability. Five replicates are preferred for
statistical robustness, especially in heterogeneous soils or when
detecting small differences between treatments.
:::

### 6.4 Backfilling

Backfill the sampling hole with surrounding soil to minimize site
disturbance and prevent tripping hazards.

### 6.5 Laboratory Processing

1. Remove the plastic caps or foil from the core
2. Transfer the entire soil core from the ring into a pre-weighed
   aluminum drying tin. Use a spatula or trowel to ensure all soil is
   transferred; scrape the inside of the ring if necessary.
3. Record the mass of the tin plus field-moist soil (this can also be
   used to calculate gravimetric moisture if a separate subsample is
   not taken)
4. Place the tin in the drying oven at 105 C for a minimum of 24 hours
   (until constant mass is achieved). See
   [SOP-L16](../lab_sops/SOP-L16-drying-ovens.qmd).
5. Remove the tin from the oven and cool in a desiccator for 20--30
   minutes
6. Weigh the tin plus oven-dried soil and record the mass


## 7. Quality Control and Acceptance Criteria

### 7.1 Calculations

**Bulk density** (g/cm^3^):

$$
\rho_b = \frac{M_{\text{dry}}}{V_{\text{core}}}
$$

where $M_{\text{dry}}$ = mass of oven-dried soil (g) and
$V_{\text{core}}$ = internal volume of the core ring (cm^3^).

**Gravimetric moisture content** (if determined from the same core):

$$
\theta_g = \frac{M_{\text{wet}} - M_{\text{dry}}}{M_{\text{dry}}}
$$

where $M_{\text{wet}}$ = mass of field-moist soil (g).

**Total porosity** (fraction):

$$
\phi = 1 - \frac{\rho_b}{\rho_s}
$$

where $\rho_s$ is the particle density, typically assumed to be
2.65 g/cm^3^ for mineral soils.

### 7.2 Expected Ranges

Typical bulk density values for mineral soils:

| Soil Type                     | Expected $\rho_b$ (g/cm^3^) |
|:------------------------------|:----------------------------|
| Well-aggregated forest or prairie topsoil | 0.8 -- 1.2        |
| Cultivated agricultural topsoil | 1.1 -- 1.5                |
| Compacted or traffic-affected soil | 1.5 -- 1.8             |
| Sandy subsoil                 | 1.4 -- 1.8                  |
| Clay-rich subsoil             | 1.1 -- 1.6                  |

Values outside the range of 0.5 -- 2.0 g/cm^3^ for mineral soils
should be investigated for sampling or measurement error.

### 7.3 QC Requirements

- Collect a minimum of three replicate cores per plot or treatment
- Calculate the coefficient of variation (CV) among replicates. A CV
  greater than 10% suggests high spatial variability or possible
  sampling problems (compaction, lost soil during extraction). Consider
  collecting additional replicates.
- Verify core ring dimensions at the start of each sampling campaign.
  If the ring is dented or deformed, replace it.
- Dry samples to constant mass. If the mass changes by more than
  0.1 g between successive weighings (at least 4 hours apart), continue
  drying.

| Dried soil              | Return to field site if uncontaminated, or standard trash |

## 10. Training Record

Before collecting bulk density cores independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Complete [SOP-F01 Field Safety](SOP-F01-field-safety.qmd) training
3. Complete [SOP-F56 Soil Sampling](SOP-F56-soil-sampling.qmd) training
4. Observe a trained operator perform core collection, trimming, and
   laboratory processing
5. Demonstrate proper core driving technique, trimming to flush, and
   capping without compacting the sample
6. Process at least three replicate cores through drying and weighing
   with a CV below 10%
7. Be signed off by the field lead or PI


## Appendix A: Example Calculation {.appendix}

```{r}
#| label: bulk-density-calc
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Bulk density calculation from core method
# Core ring dimensions
diameter_cm <- 5.0
height_cm <- 5.0
volume_cm3 <- pi * (diameter_cm / 2)^2 * height_cm

# Masses
tin_g <- 15.32             # Tare mass of aluminum tin
tin_wet_g <- 112.45        # Tin + field-moist soil
tin_dry_g <- 95.78         # Tin + oven-dried soil (105 C, 24 h)

# Calculations
mass_dry_g <- tin_dry_g - tin_g
mass_wet_g <- tin_wet_g - tin_g

bulk_density <- mass_dry_g / volume_cm3
grav_moisture <- (mass_wet_g - mass_dry_g) / mass_dry_g
porosity <- 1 - (bulk_density / 2.65)

cat(sprintf("Core volume:          %.2f cm3\n", volume_cm3))
cat(sprintf("Oven-dry soil mass:   %.2f g\n", mass_dry_g))
cat(sprintf("Bulk density:         %.2f g/cm3\n", bulk_density))
cat(sprintf("Gravimetric moisture: %.3f g/g\n", grav_moisture))
cat(sprintf("Total porosity:       %.2f\n", porosity))
```


## Appendix B: Coarse Fragment Correction {.appendix}

If the core contains gravel or rock fragments larger than 2 mm, the
bulk density of the fine-earth fraction (less than 2 mm) can be
calculated by removing the coarse fragments from the oven-dried sample,
weighing them separately, and estimating their volume:

$$
\rho_{b,\text{fine}} = \frac{M_{\text{dry}} - M_{\text{cf}}}{V_{\text{core}} - V_{\text{cf}}}
$$

where $M_{\text{cf}}$ = mass of coarse fragments (g) and
$V_{\text{cf}}$ = volume of coarse fragments (cm^3^), estimated by
water displacement or by dividing $M_{\text{cf}}$ by an assumed rock
density (typically 2.65 g/cm^3^).

Record the coarse fragment mass fraction and report whether the bulk
density value refers to the whole soil or the fine-earth fraction.


## Appendix C: Troubleshooting {.appendix}

| Symptom                       | Probable Cause                  | Corrective Action              |
|:------------------------------|:--------------------------------|:-------------------------------|
| Core compacted during insertion | Soil too dry and hard; excessive force | Moisten the surface slightly (note in field notebook); do not hammer past flush |
| Soil falls out of the bottom  | Loose sandy soil; insufficient cohesion | Try sampling when soil is slightly moist; use a core sampler with a retaining basket |
| Large roots fill the core     | Heavily rooted location          | Move to a nearby location; note the root density |
| CV among replicates exceeds 10% | High spatial variability; compaction artifacts | Collect additional replicates; inspect technique |
| Bulk density above 2.0 g/cm^3^ | Measurement error or rock fragment in core | Re-check masses and volume; inspect for gravel |
| Bulk density below 0.5 g/cm^3^ | Organic layer sampled; incomplete core | Verify that mineral soil was sampled; check for lost soil |
